hero.lead: Dry glass fabric, a little resin and the power of air: this is how a strong, light composite panel is made by vacuum infusion – from the ingredients to demoulding.
film.note: Just over a minute, with English narration and subtitles. Every frame is rendered from the 3D model below.
film.noteHu: Narration and subtitles are in Hungarian for now – an English version is coming. Every frame is rendered from the 3D model below.
what.big: We lay the fabric on the mould dry, seal it airtight under a film and suck the air out. Then we open the resin line – and the outside air pressure pushes the resin in between the layers, just as air pressure pushes a drink up a straw.
what.why: Why is this good? You get exactly as much resin as you need: the panel has more fibre and less excess resin than with hand lay-up, and hardly any air bubbles. The resin moves in a closed system, so very little vapour gets into the workshop, and the quality is repeatable from part to part.
ing.lead: What you need in the workshop, and what goes into or around the panel. For each item we also say what it is for – because leaving out any of them can ruin the part.
ing.mouldD: A flat, smooth aluminium plate. The finished part 'copies' its surface.
ing.potD: The system draws the mixed resin from here. A valve starts and stops the infusion.
ing.trapD: A container in the vacuum line. If resin overflows, it collects here instead of reaching the pump.
ing.bufferD: A vacuum reservoir between the trap and the pump. It smooths out the vacuum so it stays steady throughout.
ing.pumpD: Sucks the air out from under the film and holds the vacuum for the whole infusion.
ing.gaugeD: The gauge shows whether the vacuum is holding; the hoses connect the pot, the panel, the trap and the pump.
ing.releaseD: A thin layer on the mould so the finished panel comes off instead of sticking.
ing.fabricD: Glass, carbon or aramid fabric, stacked in the right directions. This is what makes the panel strong.
ing.peelD: Torn off at the end: it takes the consumables with it and leaves a rough surface that bonds well.
ing.meshD: The resin's 'motorway': the resin races along it over the panel and soaks down into the fabrics from there.
ing.spiralD: On one side the resin inlet, on the other the vacuum outlet.
ing.bagD: The sticky tape runs all round the edge of the mould and the film is pressed onto it: that makes the package airtight.
ing.resinD: A two-part, thin, free-flowing resin. Once mixed it only stays liquid for a limited time – so you have to work against the clock.
lay.h2: The layup, from the bottom up
lay.clickD: For each layer you can read what it is for and how thick it really is.
lay.note: The thin layers are drawn enlarged. In reality, with four fabric plies the finished panel is about 2 mm thick – and the consumables come off when it is demoulded.
lay.stays: stays on the mould surface, not part of the panel
why.release: Stops the resin sticking to the mould. Without it the finished panel would not come off.
why.glass: Reinforcement fabric. The fibre direction (0/90° or ±45°) decides which loads the panel can carry; the combination of plies gives the strength you want.
why.carbon: Carbon fabric: stiffer and lighter than glass, but more expensive.
why.peelply: Torn off at the end: it takes the mesh with it and leaves a rough, bondable surface.
why.flowmesh: The resin's fast lane: it runs along this over the panel and soaks down into the fabrics from here.
why.bag: Seals the package airtight. Under vacuum it pulls tight over the layers and compresses them.
model.lead: Drag to rotate, pinch or scroll to zoom. The buttons jump to key moments of the process.
model.alt: 3D model of a vacuum infusion set-up: table, mould, layers, vacuum bag, resin pot, resin trap, buffer tank and pump
m.lead: Nine steps. The order matters: whatever you skip will show on the finished panel.
m1.p: We clean it, then apply the release agent.
m1.w: Why? Resin sticks to everything – without release agent the panel would stay on the mould.
m2.p: The reinforcement fabrics are stacked in the planned directions (e.g. 0/90° and ±45°) and held in place with spray adhesive.
m2.w: Why? The fibre direction decides which way the panel will be strong.
m3.p: The peel ply goes on top of the fabrics, then the mesh, with the spiral tubes along the two edges.
m3.w: Why? The mesh stops a few centimetres short of the vacuum side, so the resin soaks the panel first and only then reaches the vacuum line.
m4.p: Sealant tape around the edge of the mould, the vacuum bag on top. Then the hoses are connected: pot → panel → trap → buffer tank → pump.
m5.p: We switch on the pump and the film pulls tight over the layers. Then we close it off from the pump and watch the gauge.
m5.w: Why? If the vacuum drops, the package is leaking somewhere – that would give a bubbly, weak panel. So we find the leak and seal it.
m6.p: The two components are weighed on a scale in the manufacturer's ratio and mixed, then degassed under vacuum if needed.
m6.w: Why? With the wrong ratio the resin never cures properly.
m7.p: We open the valve: the resin runs along the mesh and soaks down through the fabrics until the flow front reaches the vacuum side.
m8.p: We close the inlet, keep the vacuum on and let the resin harden.
m8.w: Why? Resin doesn't dry – it hardens through a chemical reaction, which needs time and the right temperature.
m9.p: We pull off the film; the mesh comes off together with the peel ply, and finally the panel is released from the mould. Done.
calc.h2: Will the resin get there in time?
calc.lead: Mixed resin only stays liquid for a limited time (the pot life). In that time the resin has to reach the far end of the panel. Try how the fill time changes with the panel length.
calc.pot: The white line: the resin's pot life (60 minutes in this example).
calc.formula: Estimate from Darcy's law: t ≈ μ·φ·L² / (2·K·Δp). Length counts squared: a panel twice as long takes four times as long to fill. Assumptions: resin viscosity 0.2 Pa·s, porosity 0.5, pressure difference 0.9 bar, permeability 10⁻⁹ m² with mesh, 3·10⁻¹¹ m² without (glass fabric). A rough guide, not a design calculation.
calc.v1: Fits comfortably within the pot life.
calc.v2: Only just fits – you'll need to work fast.
calc.v3: It won't fit: the resin gels before it gets to the end. You need more inlets or a slower resin.
b.lead: Stack up to twenty plies, put a load on the panel, and see how much it bends and where the first crack appears. The panel is 400 × 300 mm and rests on supports along all four edges, like a shelf board in its frame.
b.note: The bottom is the mould side. A new ply always goes on top.
b.disc: Simplified engineering estimate (classical laminate theory), not a design calculation.
matn.gl-woven: Equal in both directions, cheap, infuses well.
matn.gl-ud: Strong and stiff along the fibres only.
matn.gl-biax: Two UD sub-plies at ±45°: carries shear and twisting.
matn.gl-csm: Same in every direction but weaker; epoxy needs the powder-bound type.
matn.cf-ud: Exceptionally stiff and strong along the fibres, weak across them.
matn.ar-woven: Excellent in tension, weak in compression.
matn.core-pet: Holds the two skins apart: bending stiffness grows with the square of their spacing, for very little weight.

b.lblW: Weight in the middle of the panel, on 6 × 6 cm: {kg} kg
b.empty: No plies yet. Pick a material above, or a ready-made layup.
b.fail: This layup could not be calculated.
b.addOne: Add at least one ply and we'll start calculating.
b.atW: with a {kg} kg weight in the middle
b.over: The current load is already above this: the panel cracks at a much lower load.
b.isRef: This is our panel: everything else is compared with it.
b.vsRef: Compared with our panel: {x} in x, {y} in y.
b.early: It cracks before it bends this far.
b.center: Weight in the middle of the panel.
b.capRed: In red: the first ply has already cracked here.
b.capRing: The ring marks where the first crack would appear.
b.aCanvas: Deflection of the panel: maximum {w} mm.
e.ref: This is our panel: four plies of glass fabric, 0/90° on the outside and ±45° inside. All other layups are compared with it.
e.less: Under the same load it bends {f} less than our four-ply glass panel ({w} mm instead of {ref} mm).
e.more: Under the same load it bends {f} more than our four-ply glass panel ({w} mm instead of {ref} mm).
e.same: In bending it is about as stiff as our four-ply glass panel.
e.long: In bending it is {f} stiffer lengthwise (along the 400 mm side) than crosswise: most fibres run this way, and crosswise it is mostly the resin doing the work.
e.cross: In bending it is {f} stiffer crosswise (along the 300 mm side) than lengthwise: most fibres run this way.
e.all45: All fibres run at ±45°: the panel handles shear and twisting well, but bends more easily than if some fibres ran parallel to its edges.
e.some45: The ±45° plies carry shear and twisting: the panel twists less when the load isn't exactly in the middle.
e.asym: The layup is not mirror-symmetric about the mid-plane. During curing the plies shrink differently and the panel warps. The same plies mirrored (e.g. 0/90/90/0) would stay flat.
e.sym: The layup is mirror-symmetric about the mid-plane, so it stays flat after curing.
e.aramid: Aramid (Kevlar) is excellent in tension but weak in compression: it takes about {f} less load pushed than pulled. In bending one side of the panel is always in compression{also}. So it is better to put glass or carbon on the compression side.
e.aramidAlso: , and here too an aramid ply is the first to crack
e.foamRef: Without the foam this would be exactly our panel – so the whole difference comes from the {c} mm foam, while the weight goes up by only {p}%. The foam holds the two skins apart, and bending stiffness grows roughly with the square of their spacing (the sandwich effect).
e.foam: The {c} mm foam makes the panel {f} stiffer than the same plies without foam, while the weight goes up by only {p}%. The foam holds the two skins apart, and bending stiffness grows roughly with the square of their spacing (the sandwich effect).
e.csm: The mat is the same in every direction but weaker than fabric; with epoxy resin you need the powder-bound type, because the usual (emulsion) binder only dissolves in the styrene of polyester resin.
e.heavier: {m} kg per square metre: {f} heavier than our panel ({r} kg/m²).
e.lighter: {m} kg per square metre: {f} lighter than our panel ({r} kg/m²).
e.fpfP: The first crack appears at about {q} kPa pressure (≈ {m} kg/m², about {tot} kg on the whole panel). The panel can usually take more than this, but from here on it is damaged.
e.fpfW: The first crack appears with a weight of about {kg} kg standing in the middle. The panel can usually take more than this, but from here on it is damaged.
e.thinP: So a panel just {h} mm thin can't carry even about {kg} kg spread evenly without cracking{end}
e.thinW: So a panel just {h} mm thin can't carry even a weight of about {kg} kg without cracking{end}
e.thinRef: – that's why a real product needs more plies or a core. Try the sandwich layup!
w.asym: Asymmetric layup: the panel will warp during curing. The calculation uses the reduced bending stiffness (D* = D − B·A⁻¹·B).
w.coupling: Significant bend–twist coupling (|D16|/D11 or |D26|/D22 > 0.1): the deflection calculation ignores it, so the result is less accurate.
w.large: The deflection is more than half the panel thickness: in reality membrane action stiffens the panel, so the linear model overestimates the deflection (on the safe side).
w.core: Sandwich panel with a core: core shear deformation is treated in a simplified way, and the core's shear strength is checked separately. Skin debonding and local indentation are not modelled.
f.h2: Where the recipe can go wrong
f1.p: The most common fault. A tiny hole in the film or a badly pressed sealant tape, and air gets in: the panel ends up with bubbles and dry spots. That's why no infusion starts without a leak test.
f2.p: Without a resin trap, overflowing resin gets into the pump and wrecks it.
f3.p: If the resin doesn't reach the end within the pot life, the far end of the panel stays dry. Large parts need several inlets.
f4.p: The resin stays tacky and the panel is weak. Always weigh it, using the manufacturer's ratio.
f5.p: If the mesh reaches all the way to the outlet, the resin 'races' along it into the vacuum line before it has soaked the panel.
mk.lead: One week, one question: can vacuum infusion be explained so that anyone understands it?
mk.p1: The geometry is described by a single parameter file (layers, dimensions, equipment). Both the Fusion 360 CAD model and the Blender animation are built from it; the video frames come from Blender, the voice and music from a script. I did the work with Claude AI: it wrote the first version of the code, and I ran it, checked it and corrected its technical mistakes. The whole process, including prompts and dead ends, is in the journal below (in Hungarian).
